'''Ephraim Fischbach''' (born 1942) is an American [[physicist]] and a professor at [[Purdue University]]. He is best known for his attempts to find a [[fifth force]] of nature<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wilford |first=John Noble |date=Oct 17, 1986 |title=PHYSICISTS CHALLENGE THEORY OF A 'FIFTH FORCE' BEYOND GRAVITY |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/10/17/us/physicists-challenge-theory-of-a-fifth-force-beyond-gravity.html |work=New York Times}}</ref> and his research relating to the detection of [[Neutrino|neutrinos]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Foltz |first=Aulden |date=December 1, 2016 |title=Physicists propose new system for detecting neutrinos |url=https://stanforddaily.com/2016/12/01/physicists-propose-new-system-for-detecting-neutrinos/ |work=[[Stanford Daily]]}}</ref> He has also done work relating to the prediction of [[Solar flare|solar flares]]<ref>{{Cite news |last=WAMC Northeast Public Radio |date=November 1, 2012 |title=Dr. Ephraim Fischbach, Purdue University – Predicting Solar Flares |url=https://www.wamc.org/academic-minute/2012-11-01/dr-ephraim-fischbach-purdue-university-predicting-solar-flares |work=WAMC Northeast Public Radio}}</ref> and the detection of radiation by cell phones.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ephraim Fischbach |url=https://thebulletin.org/biography/ephraim-fischbach/ |access-date=2024-01-10 |website=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists |language=en-US}}</ref>

Fischbach studies variation in [[radioactive decay]] rates, suggesting that neutrino emission from the Sun reduces the rate of nuclear decay.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Madrigal |first=Alexis C. |date=August 25, 2010 |title=Maybe Radioactive Decay Rates Aren't Physical Constants |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2010/08/maybe-radioactive-decay-rates-arent-physical-constants/62058/ |work=[[The Atlantic]]}}</ref> He reanalysed the [[Eötvös experiment]], which he saw as evidence for a fifth physical force.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fischbach |first1=Ephraim |last2=Sudarsky |first2=Daniel |last3=Szafer |first3=Aaron |last4=Talmadge |first4=Carrick |last5=Aronson |first5=S.H. |date=6 January 1986 |title=Reanalysis of the Eötvös experiment |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.3 |journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=3–6 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.3 |pmid=10032514 |bibcode=1986PhRvL..56....3F |url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, in 1992, he and Carrick Talmadge conducted an experiment which found no compelling evidence for a fifth force.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fischbach |first1=Ephraim |last2=Talmadge |first2=Carrick |date=March 19, 1992 |title=Six years of the fifth force |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/356207a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=356 |issue=6366 |pages=207–215 |doi=10.1038/356207a0 |bibcode=1992Natur.356..207F |s2cid=21255315 |issn=0028-0836|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Fischbach has been a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] since 2001, and a professor at Purdue since 1979. He also was an associate professor at the [[C. N. Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics|Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in [[Stony Brook, New York]] from 1978 to 1979. He received a B.A. in physics in 1963 from [[Columbia University]] and a Ph.D. in 1967 from the [[University of Pennsylvania]].
